hook: Formats are **contracts**. CSV lies, JSON flexes, Parquet tells the truth — choose per workload.

scenes.title: CSV: universal, and **full of traps**
scenes.narration: CSV is the cockroach of data formats — everywhere, indestructible, and beloved by Excel users. But it carries no types: everything is a string until parsed, so a date column arrives as text and an amount as text-that-looks-like-a-number until something breaks. Encoding is the classic landmine — files claiming UTF-8 but holding Latin-1, exploding on the first accented name. Delimiters vary by locale — semicolons in Europe. Rule: parse explicitly — dtypes, encoding, delimiter — never trust defaults, and never let pandas infer silently in production.

lines: # CSV = a printout without a schema

scenes.narration: The CSV survival kit. Specify encoding and dtype mapping explicitly — inference is for exploration, not production. Watch embedded commas and newlines inside quoted fields — legit per spec, fatal to naive parsers and hand-edits. And remember what CSV fundamentally is: a printout without a schema. Two teams reading the same file can end up with different types for the same column. For anything you control, graduate to a format that carries its types with it — which is exactly where Parquet comes in.

scenes.title: JSON: the **API dialect**; JSONL: the data-pipeline dialect
scenes.sub: Nested, flexible, and why bulk workloads go line-delimited

lines: # one syntax error → whole file lost

steps.at: JSON is the language of APIs
a corrupt line costs one record
the pipeline world runs on JSONL

scenes.narration: JSON is the language of APIs — self-describing, nested, human-readable. Perfect for messages, config, and documents. But for bulk data it has two problems: parsing a giant array needs the whole thing in memory, and a single syntax error kills the entire file. Enter JSONL — JSON Lines: one complete JSON object per line. Each line independent, streamable, appendable, and a corrupt line costs one record, not the dataset. Logs, embeddings exports, eval sets, batch API requests — the pipeline world runs on JSONL.

steps.at: JSON for anything a human or an API

scenes.narration: Usage rules. JSON for anything a human or an API consumes — messages, configs, single documents. JSONL for anything a pipeline consumes — stream a line, parse, process, discard; memory stays flat regardless of file size. Compress with gzip when files travel or sit still — text compresses enormously. And validate JSONL records with Pydantic at the boundary — Stage 1's discipline applies verbatim to every line that arrives.

scenes.title: Parquet: **columnar, typed, compressed**
scenes.sub: Analytics shape: read 3 of 40 columns, pay for 3

steps.at: Columnar: data stored column by column

scenes.narration: Parquet is the analytics format, born at Twitter, now the default for data lakes and ML datasets. Three properties change everything. Columnar: data stored column by column — a query touching three of forty columns reads only those three. Typed: schema rides inside the file — no inference drift, ever. Compressed: columnar storage compresses dramatically — often ten times smaller than CSV. When you see benchmarks claiming pandas-on-Parquet reads a hundred times faster than CSV, this is why: less I/O, less parsing, zero type guessing.

steps.at: reads a file like a book

scenes.narration: The mental model. Row storage — CSV, JSON — reads a file like a book: to find one fact you scan everything. Column storage — Parquet — reads it like a spreadsheet's columns: grab exactly the columns your query names, skip the rest. Add compression that exploits column similarity and types enforced at write time. The trade-off: Parquet isn't human-readable and appends are awkward. Interchange with humans: CSV. Analytics and ML datasets: Parquet, full stop.

scenes.title: Partitioned Parquet = **folders as an index**
scenes.sub: year=2026/month=03/ — prune files you don't need
scenes.narration: Partitioning takes Parquet from good to great: you write a dataset as a folder tree where path segments encode column values — year equals 2026, month equals 03. Query engines read this like an index: ask for March and they open only March's files, skipping everything else. For time-series, logs, and event data this is the difference between reading gigabytes and megabytes. Tools: pandas via pyarrow's partition cols, Polars, DuckDB — they all write and exploit partitioned datasets natively.

do: hundreds of MB is the sweet spot

scenes.narration: Partitioning rules. One: encode the columns you filter by — date almost always, region often. Two: low cardinality — thousands of partitions each holding three rows is worse than no partitioning; the file-open overhead eats the gains. Three: mind file size — hundreds of megabytes per file is the sweet spot; if your pipeline spawns thousands of tiny files, schedule a compaction. This is data-lake literacy, and it's directly testable with DuckDB, which queries partitioned folders with plain SQL.

scenes.title: Arrow: the **shared memory** underneath
scenes.sub: Zero-copy handoffs between pandas, Polars, DuckDB, and ML frameworks

steps.at: read with Polars, analyze with DuckDB

scenes.narration: A quiet revolution: Apache Arrow defines a standard columnar memory layout. Because pandas, Polars, DuckDB, Spark, and ML frameworks all speak Arrow, data passes between them zero-copy — no serialize-parse round trips. PyArrow is Arrow's Python face, and it powers pandas' Parquet support. Practical effect: read with Polars, analyze with DuckDB, train with PyTorch — the dataframe converts in microseconds, because underneath it's the same bytes in memory. Fewer copies, less RAM, faster pipelines.

steps.at: Conversions that used to cost seconds

scenes.narration: Why you care. Conversions that used to cost seconds now cost microseconds because nothing is serialized — it's the same memory layout with different wrappers. Arrow's Parquet reader is parallel and row-group aware; when pandas reads Parquet fast, Arrow is doing the work. And if your world includes Spark or R or any Arrow-speaking system, data interchange stops being a project. Learn the name now — PyArrow appears in every performance conversation in the chapters ahead.

scenes.title: Parquet vs DB vs Vector store — **different jobs**
scenes.sub: Tables, transactions, and meaning don't share one tool
scenes.narration: The format decision, architecturally. Parquet excels at bulk analytics over immutable data — cheap, scalable, great for datasets and logs. Databases — Postgres, SQL Server — own transactions, constraints, and concurrent reads-and-writes; if data mutates and must be consistent, a database earns its cost. Vector stores own semantic search — similarity over embeddings at scale. Mature systems use all three, each where it's strongest — and DuckDB, the next reel, is the glue that queries across them.

steps.at: Analytics and ML datasets live as Parquet
Semantic search lives in a vector layer
write Parquet for analytics AND sync

scenes.narration: The three-layer picture. Operational truth lives in a database — where money moves, where constraints hold. Analytics and ML datasets live as Parquet — where scans are cheap and schemas travel with the data. Semantic search lives in a vector layer — where meaning is queryable. Your embeddings pipeline will write Parquet for analytics AND sync to a vector store for retrieval — same data, two shapes, each correct for its job. Choosing per workload is the whole lesson.

scenes.title: Now query it all — without a server
scenes.next: Reel 20 · DuckDB — SQL over files, in-process analytics

recap: CSV: explicit encoding/dtypes always; JSON for APIs, JSONL for pipelines (streamable, corrupt-line-safe)
Parquet: columnar + typed + compressed; partition by filtered columns; Arrow = zero-copy memory glue
Three layers: DB for mutating truth, Parquet for bulk analytics, vector store for meaning

quiz.q: Why is Parquet faster than CSV for analytics queries?
opts: It uses a better programming language
Columnar storage reads only the columns a query needs + compression + typed schema
It stores data on the GPU
quiz.why: Column pruning means a 3-column query over a 40-column file reads ~7.5% of the bytes; compression shrinks further; no type inference needed.

quiz.q: Why do pipelines prefer JSONL over a single big JSON array?
opts: Line-delimited records stream with constant memory, and one corrupt line kills one record, not the file
quiz.why: Each JSONL line is independent: stream-process gigabytes with flat memory, append safely, and failures are local to one record.

quiz.q: You're partitioning Parquet by a column with 2 million distinct values. What happens?
opts: Thousands of tiny files/partitions — file-open overhead swamps the pruning benefit
quiz.why: Partition on low-cardinality columns you actually filter by; high-cardinality partitioning creates the small-files problem.

code.title: Formats in practice — CSV in, Parquet out, partitioned
code.body:
import pandas as pd
import pyarrow as pa
import pyarrow.parquet as pq

# --- CSV: parse explicitly (no silent inference in prod) ----------
dtypes = {"amount": "float64", "status": "category"}
df = pd.read_csv("events.csv", encoding="utf-8", dtype=dtypes,
                 parse_dates=["created"])

# --- Parquet: typed + compressed -----------------------------------
df.to_parquet("events.parquet", index=False, compression="snappy")
# Typical result: 10x smaller than CSV, schema embedded, 10-50x faster reads

# --- Partitioned dataset: folders as an index -----------------------
table = pa.Table.from_pandas(df)
pq.write_to_dataset(
    table,
    root_path="events_lake",
    partition_cols=["status"],       # year/month for time series
)
# → events_lake/status=P1/0000.parquet  events_lake/status=P2/...
# DuckDB/pandas read only the partitions a filter touches

# --- JSONL: the pipeline interchange --------------------------------
with open("embeddings.jsonl", "w", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    for row in df.itertuples():
        f.write(json.dumps({"id": row.id, "text": row.text}) + "\n")
# Read back with constant memory:
# for line in open("embeddings.jsonl"): rec = json.loads(line)
annot: compression="snappy" — fast, moderate ratio; "zstd" for archives
partition_cols on what you FILTER by — not everything stored
json.dumps per line + streaming reads = flat memory over any file size

notes:
# File Formats

## CSV pitfalls
- No types, encoding landmines (utf-8 vs latin-1), delimiter variance, quoting traps.
- Prod rule: explicit `encoding`, `dtype`, `parse_dates` — never infer silently.

## JSON & JSONL
- JSON: APIs, config, documents (nested, flexible).
- **JSONL**: one JSON object per line — streamable, appendable, corrupt-line-safe.
- Compress text with gzip (`.jsonl.gz`).

## Parquet
- Columnar + typed schema + compressed (snappy/zstd). ~10x smaller, 10-50x faster analytics vs CSV.
- `df.to_parquet(...)` / `pd.read_parquet(...)`.

## Partitioning
- Folder tree encodes column values (`year=2026/month=03/`) → engine prunes folders.
- Partition by **filtered** low-cardinality columns; avoid the small-files problem (target ~100MB-1GB files).

## Arrow / PyArrow
- Standard in-memory columnar layout → zero-copy between pandas/Polars/DuckDB/Spark.
- Powers pandas' Parquet reader; `pa.Table.from_pandas(df)` converts in μs.

## Parquet vs DB vs Vector
| Job | Tool |
| --- | --- |
| Mutating transactional truth | Postgres / SQL Server |
| Bulk immutable analytics | Parquet (+ DuckDB) |
| Semantic similarity at scale | Vector store (Stage 4) |
